rows.message:
Represent the masking set as values, not a named map

`secretsToMask` returned a `Record<string, string>`, which meant retired
values needed names, so it invented them: `__retired_0`, `__retired_1`. Those
are legal secret names, so a session with a secret actually called
`__retired_0` had its current value overwritten by a retired one and printed
in full - the one value guaranteed not to be masked was a real, live secret.

Masking never cared about names. Every consumer immediately called
`Object.values()`. The set is now `SecretValues = readonly string[]`, so
there are no keys to collide and the bug is not fixable back into existence.
Duplicates are collapsed when the values are prepared, so two secrets sharing
a value, or a value that is both current and retired, is no longer a special
case either.

The type change is what found the last call site: the expression playground
masked against `session.config.secrets` alone, so a secret already replaced
or deleted through What-If - still present in the context being evaluated -
came back unmasked. It uses the full set now.

Converting the signatures also made the read/write split explicit: this is a
read-side view, and the type no longer lets it be mistaken for the live map
to write into, which is exactly the confusion behind the previous commit.

Verified over HTTP: a session whose secret is named `__retired_0`, after
retiring another secret, prints `***` and neither value appears anywhere in
the payload.

576 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Fixes disclosure of live and retired secrets through masking-name collisions and the expression endpoint. Include the confidentiality fix, with public wording reviewed.

rows.message:
Mask overlapping secret values as one run

Two secrets can overlap in the text - `abcdef` and `defghi` both occur in
`abcdefghi` - and masking them one value at a time destroys the evidence the
other needed. `maskSecrets` replaced sequentially, so the first match
consumed the `def` the second depended on and left `***ghi` with half a
secret in the output. `maskChunks` and `StreamMasker` shared the bug from the
other direction: they collected spans but *skipped* any that overlapped one
already found, leaving the same fragment.

The spans are now all decided first and overlapping ones merged, so a chain
of overlapping secrets redacts to a single `***`. Occurrences of one value
are scanned overlapping too (`at + 1` rather than `at + length`), so `aa` in
`aaa` covers all three characters instead of leaving a trailing one. Strictly
overlapping spans merge; merely adjacent ones do not, so two different
secrets written back to back still read as two masks.

`maskSecrets` is now built on the same range logic rather than a sequence of
replacements. Three implementations of "decide what to redact" is why one bug
appeared in three places, so there is one now.

Verified over HTTP: a step whose output contains an overlapping pair prints
`***`, and the only occurrence of the fragment left in the payload is the
user's own uninterpolated workflow source.

583 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Fixes partial secret disclosure when secret values overlap. This is a masking vulnerability rather than an internal refactor.

rows.message:
Keep secrets out of logs, not out of the data between steps

A step that wrote a secret to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` handed the next step a
literal `***`: `record.outputs` was masked at capture time, and the same
field is what `buildEvalContext` reads back as `steps.<id>.outputs`. So a
comparison against the real value failed, and any workflow that passes a
secret between steps - which is most of the reason to have secrets - behaved
differently here than on GitHub. Job outputs had it too, through
`needs.<job>.outputs`.

GitHub masks its logs, not the data flowing between steps. The split now
follows that: captured output (stdout, stderr, combined chunks, notes) is
masked where it is captured, because nothing reads it back; everything
execution reads back is stored raw and masked in `toClientLanes`, which is
where `lane.env` and `lane.extraPath` were already handled for exactly this
reason. Step outputs and job outputs join them.

One existing test asserted the masking on the engine record. Its intent - a
mock value equal to a secret must not reach the client - is unchanged and
still asserted, at the boundary rather than in the middle.

Verified over HTTP: a job output carrying a secret reaches the dependent job
intact, while the client payload shows `***` for both the step output and the
job output and contains the value nowhere in lane state.

585 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Restores raw secret-valued outputs between steps while moving masking to the client boundary. This fixes workflow correctness and changes a confidentiality boundary requiring review.

rows.message:
Bound a session's accumulated configuration, not just each patch

The What-If limits bounded one request, which is a different thing from
bounding a session. Every accepted patch adds to state that lives for the
session's lifetime, so repeating an individually-legal request grew one
session without creating another - and session-count limits only bound how
many sessions exist, not how large each one gets. Twelve 200-key patches were
accepted and left 2,400 keys and 2.4MB behind, with nothing stopping the
thirteenth.

The config a session is *created* with had no size check at all, only a shape
check, so the same state was reachable in a single request.

Both now go through one limit: 1,000 keys and 2,000,000 characters per
configuration map, counting key lengths as well as values. `applyWhatIf`
checks the state the patch *would* produce rather than the patch itself,
which matters for two reasons: it is the only way to see the accumulation,
and it keeps a delete-only patch legal at the limit, so a session that
reached it can still be brought back under. Maps are bounded separately, so
filling `env` does not make `vars` unusable.

The refusal is a 400 - it describes the request, not a conflict with session
state.

Verified over HTTP: the same loop that previously reached 2,400 keys now
stops at 1,000 with a 400, a delete patch still succeeds at the limit, the
freed room is reusable, and an oversized initial config is refused at
creation.

593 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Adds accumulated configuration and initial-configuration bounds to prevent memory abuse. Breaking judgment: previously accepted configurations above 1,000 keys or 2,000,000 characters per map now fail, so an existing large configuration can require adaptation even though the restriction is protective.

rows.message:
Bound live Claude calls with a spend, concurrency and timeout budget

The explanation endpoint is the one place this app can spend the operator's
money, and it had no bound of any kind. With `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` configured
every request reached the provider, so anyone who could reach the demo could
drive the bill, and the only limit was how fast they could send requests.

Three separate bounds, because they fail differently:

  calls per window  the actual spend cap, instance-wide
  concurrent calls  a burst holds open sockets and memory the spend cap says
                    nothing about, because none of those calls have finished
  per-call timeout  a hung call would otherwise hold a concurrency slot
                    indefinitely, turning a provider outage into one here

Window slots are taken before the call, not after it, so a burst of
concurrent requests cannot all pass the same check before any of them counts
- the same reservation-before-await shape session creation already uses. The
lease is released in a `finally`, so a failing call returns its slot.

Exhausting the budget is deliberately not an error. A live explanation is an
optional upgrade over the offline heuristics, so the endpoint falls back to
those: the feature degrades instead of breaking.

All three are env-configurable (`VIZU_AI_MAX_CALLS_PER_WINDOW`,
`VIZU_AI_MAX_CONCURRENT`, `VIZU_AI_TIMEOUT_MS`) and documented in DEPLOY.md
alongside why each one exists. A value that is not a positive integer falls
back to the default rather than reading as "unlimited", so a typo in the
deployment config cannot silently remove the bound.

The endpoint also gets its own per-visitor rate limit, tighter than the
expression playground's since each request is a deliberate click, so one
visitor cannot consume the whole instance budget before anyone else can.

Verified over HTTP with a key configured: explanations return 200 and
degrade to `source: "heuristic"`, concurrency slots are returned after each
failed provider call, and the 41st request returns 429. The spend cap and
concurrency refusals are covered by unit tests rather than over HTTP - no
billable calls were made, so the two paths are not distinguishable from
outside.

606 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Limits public AI spending, concurrency and request duration. Include operator protections and fallback behavior. Optional AI falls back to heuristics; I do not treat loss of unlimited optional calls as a supported-functionality removal.

rows.message:
Refuse dangling symlinks in path confinement

`realpath` reports ENOENT for a dangling symlink as well as for a genuinely
absent path, because it resolves the *target* and the target is what is
missing. `resolveWithin` read that as "doesn't exist yet", so the link's name
survived as part of the missing tail and was re-appended to the resolved
parent: the returned path looked confined, and the caller then wrote through
the link to wherever it pointed.

Reproduced: a dangling `dest.txt` inside the artifact store pointing at
`../OUTSIDE.txt` made `resolveWithin` return a path under the store, and
writing to it created the file outside.

`lstat` distinguishes the two cases. Succeeding there means the entry itself
exists and it was the target resolution that failed - a link resolution
cannot follow, which is exactly what the caller would do next - so it is
refused. A genuinely absent path still walks up as before, so ordinary new
files and nested new directories are unaffected.

This needs a pre-existing link in the store, so it is not reachable by an
anonymous demo visitor on its own; it is the last step of an escape rather
than a whole one. Fixed regardless: confinement that holds only when nothing
else went wrong is not confinement.

The artifact handlers now also report refused paths instead of silently
skipping them. "Copied 0 files. Success." is precisely the report that hides
a refusal from the person trying to debug, and both upload and download could
produce it.

612 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Closes a dangling-symlink path-confinement escape and reports refused artifact paths. Blocking writes outside the intended store is a security correction, not removal of legitimate artifact use.

rows.message:
Apply a pending step's own env: in the live context view

The context endpoint resolved the live environment with no step env layer, so
a step's own `env:` block was missing from the inspector until the step had
run - which is precisely when nobody needs to ask. Inspecting a pending step
showed `COLOR` absent, or still holding the workflow-level value, while
running it printed `step-red`.

The step's `env:` is the last layer GitHub applies and it is part of what
that step is given; a recorded `envBefore` already contained it, so only the
live path was wrong. It now resolves with the pending step's own `env:`,
which also means the layer is interpolated rather than shown as a template,
and that its precedence over a What-If override is visible before running
rather than discovered afterwards.

`envAfter` is unaffected and still excludes it: a step's own `env:` does not
persist to the next step, which is what that field answers.

Verified over HTTP: with a workflow-level `COLOR: workflow-red` and a step
`env: COLOR: step-blue`, the inspector shows `step-blue` before the step
runs, the step then prints `step-blue`, and `afterStepIndex=0` still reports
`workflow-red` for what follows.

615 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. The pending-step inspector now includes the step-specific environment with correct precedence. This is a visible inspection correctness fix.

rows.message:
Collapse duplicate matrix combinations into one lane

`matrix: {a: [1, 1]}` expanded to two identical combos, and an `include` can
produce a duplicate row the same way. A lane's identity is derived from its
combo's content, so two identical combos necessarily key the same lane: the
second overwrote the first in the lane map while `laneOrder` still listed
both. Two entries drove one lane and one combination vanished - the same
corruption the delimiter collision caused, reached from a different
direction.

Expansion now deduplicates by the same encoding lane ids use, which keeps a
string and the number that prints the same apart, and preserves the first
occurrence's position. Deduplicating rather than disambiguating with a
positional suffix: content-addressed lane identity is what share links rely
on to find a lane again, and two identical combos have identical `matrix`
contexts, so they would run identically anyway. GitHub does not document this
case, and a repeated axis value is an authoring mistake either way; one lane
is the reading that keeps everything downstream consistent.

Lane creation also skips an id it has already stored. Expansion is what
prevents duplicates; this keeps any future path from reintroducing a state
where `laneOrder` and `lanes` disagree, which is the invariant that actually
matters.

Verified over HTTP: `a: [1, 1]` yields one lane, one `laneOrder` entry and
one matrix row, while `a: [1, 2]` still yields two of each.

621 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Eliminates duplicate matrix lanes that corrupted lane identity. Duplicate combinations were already inconsistent; restoring one coherent lane is a bug fix rather than removal of a documented supported capability.

rows.message:
Compute hashFiles() the way GitHub does

`hashFiles()` hashed the matched files' contents end to end. GitHub hashes
each file on its own, appends the raw digest bytes in order, and takes the
final SHA-256 over that - a hash of hashes. The two give different digests
for the same files, so a cache key computed here never matched the one the
real workflow computed, which is most of the reason to look at `hashFiles()`
in a debugger.

The old algorithm was also wrong in a way that is easy to state: hashing
contents end to end gives `{"alpha", "beta"}` and `{"alphabeta"}` the same
digest. There is a test for exactly that.

The outer hash takes the raw digest bytes, not their hex text, matching the
runner, which writes `hash.digest()` straight into the outer hash. Verified
against a reference implementation of the documented algorithm written
independently of the code under test.

Two things I could not verify from here, stated rather than glossed:

  - Egress to GitHub is blocked in this environment, so this is checked
    against the documented algorithm and the runner's approach, not against
    the output of a real workflow run.
  - Order affects the result, and the runner emits matches in
    directory-traversal order rather than a sorted one. For a pattern
    matching several files across directories the digest can still differ
    from a real run. Sorting is the deterministic choice, and the
    single-file case that dominates real use - `hashFiles` over one lockfile
    - matches exactly either way.

Empty-match behaviour is unchanged and still returns "" rather than the hash
of an empty stream, with a test pinning that distinction.

626 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Corrects hashFiles digests toward GitHub parity. Existing calculated digests/cache keys can change and should be mentioned, but the promised compatibility behavior is being repaired rather than removed.

rows.message:
Bound request bodies before they are buffered

Route handlers get no body limit of their own, so every POST was an
unbounded read. The size checks that do exist - the workflow YAML cap, the
What-If patch bounds, the accumulated-config limits - all run against an
already-parsed body, which is after the memory has been spent: a 500MB
upload was fully received and parsed before the first of them could refuse
it.

`readJsonBody` is the one place every route reads its body, so the bound
lives there: 4 MiB, comfortably above the largest legitimate request (a
1,000,000-character workflow plus JSON escaping). A declared Content-Length
over the cap is refused before anything is read, and the stream is
abandoned as soon as the bytes actually received pass it, since nothing
obliges a client to send an honest header. Checked against a production
build with a 5MB body, sent both with a Content-Length and chunked without
one.

An oversized body reads as null, exactly like malformed JSON, so every
route's existing handling covers it unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Bounds body buffering to prevent memory exhaustion. The 4 MiB limit is above the stated maximum legitimate request; blocking oversized bodies does not remove a documented supported workload.

rows.message:
Refuse lane and job ids that only exist by inheritance

Lanes, jobs and secrets are plain objects indexed by strings a request
chose, and plain objects inherit: `lanes["__proto__"]` is
`Object.prototype`, and `jobs["constructor"]` is `Object`. Every lookup read
"truthy" as "exists", so those names passed as real entries, and the engine
then wrote to whatever it had been handed.

Stepping lane `__proto__` set `Object.prototype.status`. From then on every
object in the process inherited `status: "paused"`, and every response the
server built - for every visitor, on every route, the home page included -
failed with `RangeError: Invalid status code: paused`. One anonymous
request (create a session, then POST {"action":"step","laneId":"__proto__"}
to its own /control) took the whole instance down until it was restarted.
Reproduced against a production build in demo mode; the same sequence now
answers 409 "Unknown lane" and the server keeps serving.

Client-chosen keys are now looked up as own properties only, through
`findLane`, `findWorkflowJob` and `findWorkflowStep` in session.ts. They
back `requireLane` (step, continue, run-to-end, active lane) and the
context, explain, evaluate, breakpoints and mock-outputs routes.

The same flaw, reached through other inputs:

- What-If secret rotation read the "previous value" of a secret called
  `__proto__` as `Object.prototype` and retired it. Its missing `.length`
  made the retired-character tally NaN, and `NaN > limit` is never true, so
  the 500,000-character bound on retired secret values silently stopped
  applying to that session.
- `needs: constructor` passed the parser's unknown-job check unreported,
  and the graph builder then called `.push` on `Object`, failing every
  response for that session.
- `uses: constructor@v1` returned `Object` as the action's handler; the
  step "succeeded" with no outcome and no outputs.
- A job or matrix axis named `__proto__` replaced its map's prototype
  instead of being added to it, and vanished without an issue. Supporting
  the name would need null-prototype maps through the whole engine, so the
  parser now refuses it by name instead.

The breakpoint route also checks the step exists now, as mock-outputs
already did: it checked only the job, so any string was stored as a step
key, without bound, for the session's lifetime. With both routes refusing
unknown steps, the share-link opener skips an entry the server rejects
rather than failing the whole open - the token is user-editable text, and
one bad entry should cost that entry, not the session.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Fixes an anonymous process-wide prototype-pollution DoS and inherited-key lookups, plus unbounded invalid breakpoint keys. Invalid/nonexistent identifiers are refused; previously malfunctioning reserved names are not working supported workflows.

rows.message:
Stop telling people a step is stubbed when no mock was set

For a `run:` step the mock editor promises "A mocked step is not executed".
But a mock with no outputs and no failure changes nothing, so the server
deliberately drops it - and the editor said "Applied - takes effect next
time this step runs" regardless. Someone stubbing out a command with
nothing filled in was told it was stubbed, and then it ran for real.

The editor now reads back what the server actually kept. When nothing was
set it says so, and for a `run:` step that the step will run normally and
how to stub it out instead. The server's rule itself is unchanged: it is
deliberate, and covered by "treats a mock that changes nothing as no mock
at all".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Corrects a false applied-mock confirmation that could lead someone to execute a real command they believed was stubbed. The implementation changes feedback, not the existing execution rule; the execution-risk wording needs review.

rows.message:
Build a step's evaluation context once per env layer, not once per key

`resolveEffectiveEnv` rebuilt the whole evaluation context - steps, needs,
runner, and a re-interpolated `runs-on` - for every key it interpolated.
The rebuild bought nothing: the context holds `env` by reference, so one
built per layer already sees every key applied before the current one.

It did cost. Every step resolves its environment more than once, so the
cost was O(keys x context) per step, and in simulation-only mode a "run
all" is one unbroken chain of microtasks that no incoming request can get
between. Measured on a 20-step job:

  env keys   before   after
     100      48ms     7ms
   1,000     264ms    31ms
   4,000     974ms   109ms

A matrix multiplies that across lanes, so one run-all over a large `env:`
block stalled the server for every visitor for minutes.

The new layering test passes on the old code and the new, pinning that a
key still sees earlier keys both across layers and within its own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Reduces repeated environment-context construction that could stall the shared server for minutes. Treat the documented cross-visitor availability impact as security-sensitive, not merely an internal speed improvement.

rows.message:
Yield to the event loop between steps of a run

A step with nothing to wait on - every `uses:` step, and every `run:` step
in simulation-only mode - completes without leaving the microtask queue,
so a run-all of them was one unbroken chain that no incoming request could
get between. The public demo is simulation-only, so a single "run all"
held the whole server, for every visitor, until the workflow finished.

`runLaneLoop` now yields with `setImmediate` after each step. Real `run:`
execution already waits on its process at that point, so this only makes
the simulated path yield where execution would have anyway, and the
engine's existing guards for concurrent requests cover what can happen
during the yield. The one new case is re-checked right after it: a sibling
matrix lane failing and fail-fast-cancelling this one mid-run.

Checked against a production build in demo mode: a run-all over 256
matrix lanes x 30 steps with 4,000 env keys took 56s, and another
visitor's requests during it answered in 11-14ms (114ms for the home
page) instead of waiting out the whole run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Yields between simulated steps so one visitor cannot monopolize the server during run-all. This directly mitigates the documented shared-service availability problem.

rows.message:
Report an expression too deep to trace instead of throwing

The playground's traced evaluator caught errors from parsing but not from
the walk that follows it. A long chain of `!` costs the parser one stack
frame per `!` and the walk several, so at the route's 8,000-character cap
`!!!!...true` parsed fine and then overflowed the walk; the RangeError
escaped, and the public, session-free evaluate endpoint answered it with a
500. The walk is now guarded the way parsing already was, and the overflow
comes back as the expression's error. `if:` conditions and interpolation
already caught this - only the traced path didn't.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Returns an expression error for a too-deep trace instead of a request-specific 500. The diff catches the exception; there is no demonstrated process crash, data disclosure or cross-visitor denial of service here.

rows.message:
Treat constructor() and __proto__() as unknown expression functions

Built-in functions are looked up by lowercased name in a plain object, so
an inherited name that is already lowercase was found there: `${{
constructor(1) }}` ran `Object` and evaluated to `[1]`, and `__proto__(1)`
threw a raw TypeError, where GitHub reports an unrecognized function. The
lookup now takes own keys only - the same fix as the lane, job, handler
and `needs` lookups. Nothing could be written through it; this is about
answering the way a real runner does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Rejects inherited names as unknown built-in functions, matching runner semantics. The described lookup could not write through a prototype or escape execution; this is expression correctness, not a demonstrated security boundary fix.

rows.message:
Send people to "Mock this step", not What-If, for missing outputs

The note shown on every simulated third-party action said to "use What-If
(or Mock Outputs) to provide any outputs a downstream step depends on",
and github-script's said "Use What-If to mock the `result` output". What-If
sets env, vars and secrets - it has no way to set a step's outputs - so
both sent people to a panel that can't do what the note promised. They
now name the step panel's "Mock this step", which can, and a doc comment
that still called that UI "upcoming" is updated to match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Corrects visible guidance to the existing Mock this step UI; What-If cannot provide step outputs. Include the user-facing correction.

rows.message:
Mask explanation input against current secrets; validate the AI reply

Two problems at the one boundary where step data leaves the server for a
third-party API.

A value declared secret after its step ran was sent to Anthropic in the
clear. Output is masked when captured, against the secrets known at that
moment, so a token someone spots in a log and then adds in What-If is still
unmasked in the record - and selecting a failed step fetches an
explanation automatically. The README promises What-If secrets never leave
the server process. The explain route now re-masks every free-text field
against the secrets held now, via `maskExplainInput`. Checked end to end
against a production build and a local stand-in for the API: a token
recorded in stderr, then declared secret, reached the prompt as
"401 Unauthorized for ***".

The model's JSON was trusted blindly. Every field is rendered as a React
child, where an object throws, and the reply is shaped by the step's own
output - which a crafted log or a shared link's mocked stderr controls. A
steered reply could take down the debugger view for whoever selected the
step. `parseClaudeExplanation` now type-checks each field: causes without
a string title and detail are dropped, an unknown confidence reads as
"medium", and a reply with nothing usable falls back to the heuristics.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Prevents newly declared secrets from being sent in explanation prompts and validates untrusted AI response shape. External data transfer and crafted-response effects require security review.

rows.message:
Report a failed pause-on-failure toggle instead of dropping it

`onToggleBreakOnFailure` was the one action handler in DebuggerApp without
a try/catch. Sessions live in memory, so once one is reaped or the server
restarts every call answers 404; every other control shows that in the
error banner, while this one left an unhandled rejection (an error overlay
in development) and a checkbox that silently snapped back. It now reports
the error the same way its siblings do.

rows.message:
Only let What-If delete the overrides it is actually showing

The panel loads its rows once, but diffed deletions against the session's
*current* keys - so any override that reached the session after the panel
mounted was sent as `null` on the next Apply and deleted without ever
being shown. The saved-state restore applies overrides after the page
loads (and its notice sends people to What-If to re-enter secrets), and a
second tab on the same session can add them too; either way, applying an
unrelated change wiped them, and the persistence mirror then overwrote the
stored copy to match.

Deletions are now diffed against the keys the panel has shown, which
become the applied rows after each successful Apply. Removing a visible
row still deletes it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Stops an unrelated What-If apply from deleting overrides that the panel never displayed. This repairs user configuration integrity; no secret exposure or unauthorized cross-session access is described.

rows.message:
Put the playground's error caret under the character it means

The playground invites pasting an expression "straight from a workflow
file, ${{ }} wrapper and all", and the server strips that wrapper before
parsing - so the error position came back against the unwrapped text, and
the caret drawn under the original landed four or more columns early, in
exactly the use the panel advertises. `unwrapExpression` now returns the
source together with its offset in the text as sent, and the route maps
the position back before answering.

Two client-side problems made it worse. The caret was drawn under the
live textarea, not the text that was evaluated, so editing afterwards
slid it onto other characters; and for a multi-line expression it was
drawn on a line after all of the text, at a column counted from the very
start. It is now drawn on the error's own line of the evaluated text. A
Cmd/Ctrl+Enter while an evaluation is in flight - which bypasses the
disabled button - is ignored rather than racing it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Places expression-error carets correctly for wrappers, multiline inputs and subsequent edits; also avoids duplicate evaluations. This is a user-visible debugging fix.

rows.message:
Don't crash the debugger on a job with no steps

The parser deliberately keeps a job whose `steps:` is empty or missing
("treated as an immediate success"), and the debugger's initial selection
for its lane is step 0. StepDetailPanel only checked that the selected
lane existed, then read `step.name` off a step that doesn't - a TypeError
that took down the whole debugger page on load whenever such a job was
the first lane. It now shows a placeholder instead. The other components
that index a lane's steps already guard this.

Stop telling demo visitors their run: steps execute on the server

The home page footer said, unconditionally, that `run:` steps "execute
for real in a scratch workspace on this machine". On a simulation-only

server it says the wrong, alarming thing. The page already fetches the
deployment mode for the working-tree section; the footer now uses it too,
and says what actually happens there: the command is shown, not run, and
a mock decides the result.

rows.message:
Add an app icon and make the graph's zoom controls visible

Two visual gaps a real browser session surfaced:

- The app had no favicon, so every page load fetched /favicon.ico and got
  a 404 (a console error on an otherwise clean page). Added an app/icon.svg
  - a step glyph in the app's accent blue - which Next serves as the icon
  link, so the tab has a mark and the 404 is gone.

- React Flow's zoom/fit controls default to a white background with a glyph
  colour of `inherit`, which on the dark canvas rendered as invisible
  white-on-white boxes (and washed out on the light theme). The library
  only themes them under a `.react-flow.dark` class this app never sets,
  and its stylesheet loads after globals.css, so plain overrides lose on
  load order. Feeding the `--xy-controls-button-*` variables it reads (the
  non-default names, which it never defines itself, so there is no tie)
  themes them from the app's own tokens in both light and dark. Verified in
  a headless browser: dark icons on light-raised, light icons on
  dark-raised, both legible.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AsezdaKxDMcEXG9RRhBgY

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Makes graph zoom/fit controls legible in both themes and adds the missing app icon. Include visible usability changes; no security or compatibility boundary changes.

rows.message:
Disable run controls while a shared session awaits consent

`controlAvailability` gates both the TopBar buttons and the keyboard
shortcuts, and its whole point is that a control is never offered when
firing it would only surface an engine error banner. It didn't account
for a shared session awaiting execution consent: the engine refuses every
control path until the visitor consents, but Step/Continue/Run to end/Run
all stayed enabled, so clicking one (or pressing its shortcut) produced
exactly that "hasn't been allowed to run yet" banner. The consent banner
itself even told the user these were "refused until you allow execution"
while leaving them clickable. They're now disabled until consent, which
the separate "Allow execution" button still grants.

label.note: AI-authored draft under owner authorization. Disables controls until shared-session consent, matching the pre-existing server refusal. This repairs UI availability rather than introducing an execution-consent security guarantee.

rows.message:
Add release classification evaluation harness and harden flag detection (#34)

* Add release classification evaluation harness and baseline

Labeled-case harness with inclusion, category, security-recall and
breaking-recall metrics, a 74-case synthetic corpus, and a regression
ratchet at the measured baseline. Maintainer-reviewed cases are tracked
separately and held to a stricter bar.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011FnobGT5N345tbZeisg5jN

* Fix security and breaking-change misses in release classification

Flag SSRF, XXE, open redirect, privilege escalation, sanitization and
secret exposure as security-sensitive, and explicit prose breaking
markers ([BREAKING], BREAKING:, backwards-incompatible). Bare 'breaking',
memory leaks and non-credential tokens stay unflagged. Corpus grows to 89
cases with guard cases; ratchet tightened to 0 security/breaking misses.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011FnobGT5N345tbZeisg5jN

* Harden release classification evaluation and flag detection

Evaluation: add security/breaking positive and false-alarm counts, report
empty ratios as N/A, keep accepted mismatches scored and pin them by id,
assert required positives and protected negatives per case, and require
provenance for maintainer-reviewed cases.

Detection: move flags to flags.ts with documented normalization (CRLF/CR/
LS/PS to LF, NFKC, Unicode dashes and spaces, zero-width removal), join
wrapped lines for exposure phrases, add timing attack, buffer overflow,
zip slip, prototype pollution and deserialization, symmetric noun/verb
secret exposure with credential-qualified tokens, BREAKING CHANGES and
[breaking-change] at declaration positions, support-removal forms, and
avoid/prevent context for backwards-incompatible.

Corpus is 136 synthetic cases; no real-world accuracy is claimed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011FnobGT5N345tbZeisg5jN

* Fix R9-R13 review findings in release flag detection and evaluation

Detection: restore api[ -]?keys? as its own alternative, recognize
log/logs as exposure vocabulary, stop treating a leading fix as evidence
of preserved compatibility, apply negation to support-removal phrases
(avoid/prevent/do not/don't), and treat whitespace-only lines as paragraph
breaks before joining wrapped lines.

Evaluation: add a reviewed-case gate that requires every stated label and
well-formed provenance (a pointer, not proof of review), report accepted
and unaccepted failures separately, and keep the original 'token leaked in
logs' and 'keys exposed in logs' reproductions as pending accepted misses
beside their parser-token and object-key negatives. Corpus is 156
synthetic cases; no real-world accuracy is claimed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011FnobGT5N345tbZeisg5jN

* Scope negation by clause and line in breaking-change detection

A semicolon or period now ends negation context, and a line break carries
a negator only when the previous line ends on it. Breaking checks run on
line-structured text, with phrases allowed one line wrap, so a new line
declaring support removal no longer borrows the previous line's 'prevent'.
The 30-character window is unchanged.

Adds required positives (fix: prevent crashes; drop support for Node 16 and
variants, a new-line declaration, a wrapped phrase) and negatives (do not,
avoid, prevent end of support, wrapped negators). The bare token/key and
runtime-incompatibility questions remain pending maintainer decisions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011FnobGT5N345tbZeisg5jN

* Make negation scan linear and allow spaces around one line wrap

R15: negated() searched back to the previous newline for every match, which
is quadratic on a long single line (about 30 s for 50,000 repeats). Line
starts are now computed once per scan and a pointer advances monotonically.
Clause rules and the 30-character window are unchanged. Regression tests
cover both 50,000-repeat inputs (stay unflagged within budget) and a late
new-line declaration (still found).

R16: phrases may wrap once with optional spaces on either side of the break;
blank and whitespace-only lines still never match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011FnobGT5N345tbZeisg5jN

* Remove quadratic backtracking from the trailing-negator check

TRAILING_NEGATOR used [ \t]*[,:]?[ \t]*$, whose two space runs could split the
same spaces many ways when the final anchor failed: 64,000 spaces took ~4.8 s
and 128,000 took ~19 s. Punctuation is now mandatory inside the optional
group, so each space has one parse. Negation semantics are unchanged.

Adds regression tests for the exact reproduction at several sizes (both the
support-removal and incompatibility paths), the preserved negatives, the
omitted 'This is backwards\n incompatible' R16 case, and a hostile-shape
guard. Performance wording now states what was measured, not a universal
guarantee.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011FnobGT5N345tbZeisg5jN

* Flag bare token/key exposure through logs or traces

A bare token/key becomes security-sensitive only when, within one clause
and bounded distances, the noun, exposure wording (leak, expose, disclose,
dump, print, logging/logged) and a logging destination (logs, log output,
logging output, traces) all appear. Decided by the repository owner:
missed disclosures cost more than a manual review.

Promotes the three original reproductions to required security positives
and removes their accepted exceptions. Parser-token and object-key
negatives stay protected, with new controls (token counts in logs, format
object keys in logs, log object keys to the logs). 'object keys leaked in
logs' is an accepted, documented trade-off. A flagged change is withheld
from customer notes and AI prompts; tests cover that, wrapped lines, CRLF,
paragraph breaks and long inputs. Sanitize and runtime-incompatibility
decisions remain pending.
